label: craft-floor-10y
_why: THE CRAFT HIRING-FLOOR PROBE (user go-ahead 2026-09-30 evening: 'Yes, go with a 10-year probe and report on differences. If only possible with a longer probe, do that one instead'), on the COMBINED book the same message ruled ('From now on, combine them always') with the RULED staffing ('The one with the machinists'). Run 1 = config/mod_config.artmerge6.json: the craft book artisan6 (ruled staffing) plus the six merges of merge6, proven by field diff to be exactly artisan6 + the merge keys and merge6 + the craft keys. Run 2 = config/mod_config.artmerge6-floor.json: the same plus ONE key, min_productivity_to_hire 0.01 on bg_pmr_crafts, the per-group override of the engine's BUILDING_DEFAULT_MIN_EARNINGS_TO_HIRE_EMPLOYEES (3: 'non-subsidized buildings will not hire if it would result in their annual earnings/employee falling below this threshold'; vanilla sets 10 on its owner buildings). 0.01 and not 0, because for some group fields the engine reads 0 as unset. The two builds differ in that one line and the generated header comments. WHY TEN YEARS IS ENOUGH: in the 30-year craft run (20260930_181601 run 1, artisan6 alone) world craft staffing fell 95.6% (1837) -> 88.5% (1846), and 30-45% of craft levels sat in country cells whose value added per worker was under the 3-pound floor in 1837-1848, against ~10% after 1849 — the floor binds most in exactly these years (FINDINGS F185). Second baseline seed = that run read at the same dates (no merges, but merges act only from ~1845). A probe: one seed per arm, no register reading.

_questions.Q1: World craft staffing (staffed / levels) by year, and the staffing of the crafts CONSTRUCTED since 1836, at 1846.1.1 in both arms (craft_fill.mjs --built on the kept end saves; the summaries for the path).
_questions.Q2: The hiring states of the understaffed crafts at 1846 (craft_fill.mjs: laying off / failed to hire / paused / ramping) — does 'failed to hire', the floor's signature, shrink in the floor arm, and what is left?
_questions.Q3: The crafts' economics in both arms: value added per employee (against 3), profit per revenue, wage per the country's normal rate, inbound hires.
_questions.Q4: Side effects: world GDP (displayed and at base prices), population, W and U* (world and shortlist), unemployment and peasants in the craft-heavy countries, craft goods' prices in the instrumented markets.
_questions.Q5: Craft construction 1836 -> 1846 in both arms (construction_spend.mjs): levels built, points, and the empty share.
_questions.Q6: Load and health: the init marker, no error line naming our files, clock advancing, crashes resumed.

_predictions.Q1: baseline world craft staffing at 1846 in 86-91% (the 30-year run read 88.5%); the floor arm +2 to +6 points; constructed crafts 45-65% staffed in the baseline, +5 to +20 points in the floor arm
_predictions.Q2: failed-to-hire unstaffed levels at least halved in the floor arm; laying off and paused not smaller (the margin rules are untouched, and more hires at cut wages feed the SoL-based layoffs); many new crafts still stop near 10% employment in both arms, where the pause rule (under 20% profit, at least 10% employed) binds
_predictions.Q3: value added per employee LOWER on average in the floor arm's crafts (it hires in the low-price cells the floor used to shut), margins similar or lower, wages per normal similar
_predictions.Q4: world GDP within +-3% of the baseline (inside one seed's noise); unemployment including peasants a little lower in the craft-heavy periphery; craft goods a little cheaper there
_predictions.Q5: craft construction similar in both arms; the floor arm's constructed crafts less empty

_cost: 2 runs x 1836 -> 1846, about 12-16 minutes each plus builds and harvest
_caveats: Launch ONLY through tools/testbed/launch_detached.ps1 CALLED DIRECTLY from the PowerShell tool (landmine L30).
One seed per arm: a difference larger than the path the 30-year run's crafts took (95.6 -> 88.5% in ten years) is a reading, a smaller one is noise until repeated.
No stop watcher: a probe has no end state for the register to judge.
